# 5.1 Introduction

## What You'll Learn in this Chapter

Welcome to Chapter 5! Now that we've studied arguments with
subconclusions, dependent reasons and independent reasons, we're able to
analyze and evaluate almost any argument. In approaching some pieces of
reasoning, however, we might be faced with an unexpected difficulty: in
real-life, authors might not explicitly state one or more of their
subconclusions and sometimes they might not explicitly state their
ultimate conclusions either. Thus, in this chapter:

You'll learn more about analyzing arguments. In particular, you'll learn

-   how to find missing ultimate conclusions and
-   how to find missing subconclusions.

You'll learn more about evaluating arguments. In particular, you'll
learn

-   how to evaluate inferences by supplying missing subconclusions.

You'll learn more about constructing arguments. In particular, you'll
learn

-   how to leave some conclusions unstated in arguments of your own

## A Word About Missing Conclusions

So far, we've seen how to map arguments, and we've found it useful to
compare an argument map to a map that shows us how to reach a golden
boulder.

Sometimes, the maps are very small. There's a golden boulder, a starting
boulder, and a bridge between them. These are arguments that have an
ultimate conclusion, a premise, and an inference.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_simple.png){.illustration width=140px fig-alt="A gray starting boulder with a single ladder leading up to a golden boulder."}

Sometimes, intermediate boulders are needed. These are arguments with
subconclusions.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_subconclusion.png){.illustration width=110px fig-alt="A ladder leads from a starting boulder up to an intermediate boulder, and a second ladder leads from there up to the golden boulder."}

Sometimes, boulders need to work together. These are arguments with
dependent reasons.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_dependent.png){.illustration width=180px fig-alt="Two gray boulders side by side, joined by a plank bridge. A single ladder rises from the bridge to the golden boulder."}

Sometimes, there are independent paths. These are arguments with
independent reasons.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_independent.png){.illustration width=160px fig-alt="Two separate gray boulders, each with its own ladder leaning up to the golden boulder."}

And very often, a map is composed of all these relationships.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_combined.png){.illustration width=300px fig-alt="A larger map combining all of these. A ladder rises to the golden boulder from a bridge joining two boulders. The left boulder is reached by a ladder from another bridged pair, one of which is reached by a ladder from a starting boulder below. The right boulder is reached by two independent ladders from two boulders."}

Now imagine what would happen if one of the intermediate boulders, and
the bridges that link to it, were removed. Anyone who tried to reach the
golden boulder would be stuck because the intermediate boulders and
bridges would be out. We'd be faced with three disconnected parts.

![](/images/ch05/boulders_missing.png){.illustration width=300px fig-alt="The same map with the bridged pair of boulders just below the golden boulder removed. The golden boulder floats out of reach above two separate groups of boulders, and a puzzled stick figure stands on one of the bridges."}

Exactly the same thing can happen in an argument when a sub-conclusion
is unstated!

Consider, for example, the following mapped argument:

> "(1) Argument mapping is useful. This is because (2) arguments are
> composed of claims and connections so (3) to understand an argument,
> we need to understand the claims and connections that compose it. (4)
> Argument mapping helps us to understand the claims and connections
> that compose an argument which means that (5) argument mapping helps
> us to understand arguments. (6) It's useful to understand arguments.
> For one thing, (7) understanding arguments helps us to understand
> people who disagree with us. For another thing, (8) understanding
> arguments helps us to decide if we should change our minds."

![The full argument map.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-full width=100% fig-alt="Argument map concluding: (1) Argument mapping is useful. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-full"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

This might not be the easiest argument to map, but I'm confident that
you would be able to map it, at least in part because I've stated all
of the subconclusions.

But suppose the author of this argument doesn't state claim 5, like so:

> "(1) Argument mapping is useful. This is because (2) arguments are
> composed of claims and connections so (3) to understand an argument,
> we need to understand the claims and connections that compose it. (4)
> Argument mapping helps us to understand the claims and connections
> that compose an argument. (6) It's useful to understand arguments.
> For one thing, (7) understanding arguments helps us to understand
> people who disagree with us. For another thing, (8) understanding
> arguments helps us to decide if we should change our minds."

This would give us an argument map with three disconnected parts.

![Part 1 of the disconnected map.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_1_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-part1 width=45% fig-alt="Argument map consisting of the single claim: (1) Argument mapping is useful. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-part1"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_1_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

![Part 2 of the disconnected map.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_2_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-part2 width=65% fig-alt="Argument map with a blank conclusion. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-part2"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_2_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

![Part 3 of the disconnected map.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_3_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-part3 width=60% fig-alt="Argument map concluding: (6) It's useful to understand arguments. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-part3"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Part_3_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

Without claim 5, it would be hard to see how these argument modules are
linked to each other because the natural connections (or bridges)
between them will be out.

There are two ways to solve this problem.

First, we could treat claims 3, 4, and 6 as a set of three dependent
reasons, like so:

![Claims 3, 4, and 6 treated as three dependent reasons.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_3_DR_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-three-dr width=100% fig-alt="Argument map concluding: (1) Argument mapping is useful, with claims 3, 4, and 6 as three dependent reasons. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-three-dr"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_3_DR_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

*However*, as we saw in Chapter 2, we naturally combine claims *two at a
time*. (Remember that math problem, 7 + 4 + 3 + 5 = 19? You almost
certainly added these numbers together two at a time.) Consequently,
seeing that claims 3, 4, and 6 should be combined in this way requires
us to do something that we do not naturally do.

In other words, this first way to solve our problem is hard.

Second (and this is usually the *much* better option), we can *supply
that missing conclusion ourselves and rebuild the bridges!*

![The map with the missing subconclusion, claim 5, supplied.](/images/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Unstated_S_AM_Is_Useful.png){#fig-5-1-supplied width=100% fig-alt="Argument map concluding: (1) Argument mapping is useful, with the unstated subconclusion (5) supplied. A full text description is provided."}

::: {.map-outline fig="fig-5-1-supplied"}
{{< include /outlines/ch05/CH_5_Intro_1_Unstated_S_AM_Is_Useful_list.md >}}
:::

We've actually been training for this since Chapter 3, where I noted
that we should fill in the claim that follows from two dependent reasons
as soon as we have decided that two claims [are]{.underline} dependent
reasons.

If we follow this advice, we'll naturally supply missing conclusions as
we go along, whether the missing conclusion is a subconclusion (as
above) or the ultimate conclusion itself!

Let's see how this works by walking through some examples!
